Looking at this problem, I need to determine for which real $p$ the integral $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |\log|x||^p\,dx$ converges.

**Answer- Leak Self-Check:** The problem text contains no leaked solutions, answer values, or proof sketches. Proceeding to solve.

---

## Proof

**Reduction to a one-dimensional integral.** The integrand $|\log|x||^p$ is radial (depends only on $r = |x|$). Passing to polar coordinates, $dx = \omega_n\, r^{n-1}\,dr$ where $\omega_n = |S^{n-1}|$ is the surface area of the unit sphere. Thus

$$\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |\log|x||^p\,dx = \omega_n \int_0^\infty |\log r|^p\, r^{n-1}\,dr.$$

Since the integrand is nonnegative, convergence is equivalent to finiteness. We split the integral at $r=1$, where the two sources of divergence are: the singularity at $r=0$ (where $\log r \to -\infty$) and the behavior at $r=\infty$ (where $\log r \to +\infty$).

---

**Part I — near the origin:** $\displaystyle\int_0^1 |\log r|^p\, r^{n-1}\,dr$.

On $(0,1)$ we have $\log r < 0$, so $|\log r| = -\log r$. Substitute $u = -\log r$, i.e.\ $r = e^{-u}$, $dr = -e^{-u}\,du$:

$$\int_0^1 (-\log r)^p\, r^{n-1}\,dr = \int_0^\infty u^p\, e^{-(n-1)u}\, e^{-u}\,du = \int_0^\infty u^p\, e^{-n u}\,du = \frac{\Gamma(p+1)}{n^{p+1}},$$

which is a standard Gamma-type integral. It **converges if and only if $p > -1$** (for $p \leq -1$ the singularity at $u=0$ is non-integrable: $u^p$ with $p \leq -1$ is not integrable near $0$).

---

**Part II — near infinity:** $\displaystyle\int_1^\infty |\log r|^p\, r^{n-1}\,dr$.

On $(1,\infty)$ we have $\log r > 0$, so $|\log r| = \log r$. Substitute $u = \log r$, i.e.\ $r = e^u$, $dr = e^u\,du$:

$$\int_1^\infty (\log r)^p\, r^{n-1}\,dr = \int_0^\infty u^p\, e^{(n-1)u}\, e^{u}\,du = \int_0^\infty u^p\, e^{n u}\,du.$$

For $n \geq 1$, the factor $e^{nu}$ grows exponentially. For **every** real $p$, the integrand $u^p e^{nu} \to +\infty$ as $u \to \infty$; in particular it does not even tend to zero. Hence

$$\int_0^\infty u^p\, e^{n u}\,du = +\infty \qquad \text{for all } p \in \mathbb{R}.$$

---

**Conclusion.** The full integral is the sum (up to the constant $\omega_n$) of Parts I and II. Part II diverges for **every** $p \in \mathbb{R}$. Since the integrand is nonnegative, divergence of any part implies divergence of the whole.

Therefore the integral $\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |\log|x||^p\,dx$ **diverges for every real number $p$**, and the set of such $p$ is

$$\boxed{\emptyset}.$$
